claims.planned: Docker auto-generates and loads a default profile 'docker-default' for containers on AppArmor-enabled hosts; it is 'moderately protective'
claims.finding: Both parts verbatim. Generation detail: 'The Docker binary generates this profile in tmpfs and then loads it into the kernel.' The profile applies to containers, not to the daemon. Full 'moderately protective' sentence: 'It is moderately protective while providing wide application compatibility.' (the same sentence Docker uses for the seccomp profile). The template now lives at github.com/moby/profiles (apparmor/template.go). Override per container with --security-opt apparmor=<profile>; --privileged 'Disables the default AppArmor profile' (run reference) and 'Privileged containers without an explicit AppArmor profile use unconfined'. Applicability caveat: AppArmor is an Ubuntu/Debian/SUSE-family LSM; this machine's Docker Desktop VM lists only seccomp and cgroupns under `docker info` Security Options (no apparmor), so nothing here can be demonstrated locally.
claims.quote: Docker automatically generates and loads a default profile for containers named `docker-default`. The Docker binary generates this profile in `tmpfs` and then loads it into the kernel.
claims.location: Docker Docs, 'AppArmor security profiles for Docker' (intro)

extra_findings.finding: What AppArmor is, in Docker's words.
extra_findings.quote: AppArmor (Application Armor) is a Linux security module that protects an operating system and its applications from security threats. To use it, a system administrator associates an AppArmor security profile with each program. Docker expects to find an AppArmor policy loaded and enforced.
extra_findings.location: Docker Docs, 'AppArmor security profiles for Docker' (intro)

extra_findings.quote: The `docker-default` profile is the default for running containers. It is moderately protective while providing wide application compatibility. [...] When you run a container, it uses the `docker-default` policy unless you override it with the `security-opt` option.
extra_findings.location: Docker Docs, 'AppArmor security profiles for Docker' → 'Understand the policies'

extra_findings.finding: NEW (not folklore): since Docker Engine 29.8 the daemon can generate docker-default from a custom template.
extra_findings.quote: Starting with Docker Engine 29.8, you can configure the daemon to generate the `docker-default` profile from a custom template. This changes the policy for containers that use `docker-default`. Privileged containers without an explicit AppArmor profile use `unconfined`
extra_findings.location: Docker Docs, 'AppArmor security profiles for Docker' → 'Customize the default profile'

extra_findings.finding: What docker-default actually denies (from the built-in template): all mount operations; writes to /proc outside /proc/<pid> and most of /proc/sys; /proc/sysrq-trigger and /proc/kcore entirely; writes under /sys (except the cgroup fs path pattern); /sys/firmware, /sys/kernel/security; AF_ALG and AF_VSOCK sockets; ptrace only between processes of the same profile. It allows `network`, `capability`, `file`, `umount` broadly — i.e. it is a targeted deny-list on top of general allow rules.
extra_findings.quote: deny @{PROC}/* w,   # deny write for all files directly in /proc (not in a subdir) [...] deny @{PROC}/sysrq-trigger rwklx, deny @{PROC}/kcore rwklx, deny mount, [...] deny /sys/firmware/** rwklx, [...] deny /sys/kernel/security/** rwklx,

extra_findings.finding: Debugging: denials appear in the kernel log (dmesg) as audit lines with apparmor="DENIED" and profile="docker-default"; aa-status lists loaded profiles.
extra_findings.quote: You can use `dmesg` to debug problems and `aa-status` check the loaded profiles.
extra_findings.location: Docker Docs, 'AppArmor security profiles for Docker' → 'Debug AppArmor'

extra_findings.finding: Docker's view of LSM profiles as an extra net overlapping capabilities.
extra_findings.quote: we ship a template that works with AppArmor and Red Hat comes with SELinux policies for Docker. These templates provide an extra safety net (even though it overlaps greatly with capabilities).
extra_findings.location: Docker Docs, Docker Engine security, 'Other kernel security features'

extra_findings.finding: EXECUTED — this host has no AppArmor in the Docker VM (Security Options lists only seccomp and cgroupns).
extra_findings.quote:
$ docker info | grep -A3 'Security Options'
 Security Options:
  seccomp
   Profile: unconfined
  cgroupns
extra_findings.location: executed (docker info); Docker Desktop (macOS, arm64), Engine 28.1.1, kernel 6.10.14-linuxkit, cgroup v2, containerd snapshotter 'overlayfs'

teaching_notes: Confirmed as planned. Keep the page honest about scope: AppArmor only exists on hosts whose kernel/distro enables it (not in Docker Desktop's VM here), so describe rather than demo. The interesting concrete content is the template: `deny mount`, /proc and /sys write denials, kcore/sysrq-trigger — a third, path-based layer over capabilities and seccomp (e.g. mount is denied three times over). New since folklore: template moved to moby/profiles; Engine 29.8 allows a custom docker-default template; the template denies AF_ALG/AF_VSOCK sockets.
